newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-BRAZIL PAVES WAY FOR OIL, GAS BONANZA.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BRAZIL PAVES WAY FOR OIL, GAS BONANZA.

text.p: Brazil gave the green light for private companies to move into the country's underdeveloped petroleum industry Wednesday when President Fernando Henrique Cardoso signed a law opening up the sector to competition.
Mines and Energy Minister Raimundo Brito said he expected a first batch of joint-ventures between former monopoly Petrobras and private groups to be signed by the end of the year.
"The first partnerships involving Petrobras, be they in exploration and production or in chemical or gas production will take place within 120 days as of now," Brito told reporters.

While the law allows private companies to compete against Petrobras throughout the industry, most newcomers are expected to join forces with the state-owned giant which has spent 40 years producing and exploring for oil and gas in Brazil. Petrobras has already received scores of proposals for joint-ventures, most of them in exploration and production. The projects, which involve some of the world's leading petroleum companies, would require about $3 billion in investment over the next three years, Petrobras officials say.

Brito said the opening up of the industry would boost Brazil's oil production from about 925,000 barrels per day now to 1.2 million bpd next year and 1.5 million bpd by 2000. As a result, imported petroleum would fall to about 25 percent of total consumption, down from about 40 percent now, the minister said.

Petrobras president Joel Renno said the company was also finalising details of its involvement in three major downstream projects. For a first time, Petrobras would take a minority stake of about 30 percent in each project, he said.

They involved construction a 450 mega-watt, gas-fired power station in Sao Paulo state, a new petrochemical complex to produce propane and polyethylene also in Sao Paulo and a new naphtha plant at an existing petrochemical complex in Bahia.
Another imediate task ahead of Petrobras is the selection of areas where it is currently involved in exploration and which it will seek to maintain for its own exclusive use.

Under the new law, Petrobras may only retain areas where it has already invested significantly in exploration. Areas where it has not yet exercised exploration rights will be submitted to a new National Petroleum Agency, to be set up within 120 days.
Renno said Petrobras was close to announcing which areas it wanted to keep but declined to give any estimate as to how much of Brazil's estimated 14 billion-barrel reserves those areas accounted for.
